How Tepera counts time and why it\'s built this way.

Online time and the day structure are counted through Android\'s system "Usage access" permission (Settings → Special access, not a pop-up dialog). The permission only grants access to app names and the moments they move to the foreground or background. Without it, manual activity logging keeps working fully — Tepera just won\'t have automatic Online time.\n\nTepera does not see screen content: not message text, not what you\'re actually reading or watching, not scrolling inside an app — a minute of reading looks the same as a minute of scrolling a feed. All data stays on the phone; the only network request is the "Suggest a feature" button, which opens the browser, not Tepera itself.

When enough time passes between uses of the phone, Tepera offers to label that gap with an activity — that\'s the pause card on Home. The threshold is set by three levels (Less often / Normal / More often) in Settings, with no need to understand the algorithm\'s numbers. Labeling is a suggestion, not a tracking log — a pause you leave unlabeled is never recorded as a metric.\n\nThe delay (Settings → Apps with a delay) is a manual feature: you choose the app and the wait time yourself. Android doesn\'t let apps actually block another app from launching, so the delay works through a pinned shortcut with a pause before launch — the original app icon stays in place and still opens it instantly. This is a deliberate delay you set for yourself, not a technical barrier — turning the delay off for the day is one tap, no explanation needed.

The sleep window (Settings → Time and day boundaries) doesn\'t show sleep as an activity and says nothing about how much or how well you slept. It\'s only a time range excluded from the calculation: minutes inside the sleep window don\'t count toward the day structure, don\'t become pauses, and don\'t count toward the unlock counter.
Why there are no notifications, streaks, or scores

Tepera doesn\'t send notifications trying to pull you back, doesn\'t count day streaks, and doesn\'t award points or badges for usage. The numbers on screen are facts about time that has already passed, not a goal to reach — that\'s why the app never says "goal," only "reference," and colors never turn "alarming" no matter how much time has passed. Comparisons are only ever against your own history, never against other people\'s averages.

What is known about scrolling and dopamine
This is not advice and not an assessment. It is only what science knows right now, and where scientists disagree with each other.
Scrolling means moving through a feed with no goal set in advance. Tepera can\'t see what happens inside an app: a minute of reading and a minute of scrolling look the same to it.

Neuroscientists usually describe dopamine as part of a system tied to anticipating rewards and to learning, not as a \"pleasure hormone\". Feeds that keep refreshing are built so that the next item is unknown in advance — that is a described property of the design, not a verdict on a person.

There is no single answer on whether regular social media use can be called an addiction. There is also no agreement on how strongly screen time is linked to wellbeing: some researchers see a noticeable link, others a very weak one, and others think the direction of the link is not established.

Whether \"social media addiction\" is a separate condition. Whether screen time changes wellbeing, or people with a certain wellbeing spend more time in apps. Whether the time itself matters, or what a person does during it.
Tepera draws no conclusions about you from these questions. It only shows how you use your phone; what to do with that is up to you.
